title: AI Calorie-Tracking Apps Undercount by Hundreds of Calories, NIH Study Finds
excerpt: Photo-based nutrition apps underestimated meal calories by 250 to 345 on average, with fat miscounted by about 30 grams — and the errors are worse for mixed dishes common in Indian cuisine.
body:
• An NIH study of 102 controlled meals found four popular photo-based calorie apps underestimated calories by 250–345 per meal and fat by ~30 grams.
  • AI apps struggle most with mixed dishes and culturally diverse foods — a separate University of Sydney study found calorie errors of up to 76% on Asian dishes like pearl milk tea.
  • Portion weight, not nutritional knowledge, is the core weakness: AI models often confuse cooked and dry food states, potentially tripling calorie estimates for staples like rice.
  • Experts recommend cross-checking app estimates with manual portion inputs and consulting dietitians for accurate tracking.

If you've been religiously photographing your meals and trusting an app to count your calories, new research suggests you may be eating significantly more than the numbers show. A study from the National Institutes of Health found that four popular photo-based calorie-tracking apps underestimated the calorie content of meals by roughly a third.

The NIH Study: Controlled Kitchen, Real Errors

Presented at NUTRITION 2026, the flagship meeting of the American Society for Nutrition held July 25–28 in National Harbor, Maryland, the study used 102 meals prepared in a controlled metabolic kitchen at the NIH Clinical Center. Every ingredient was weighed to the nearest 0.1 gram, providing a precise reference against which to test the apps.

Researchers ran standardised photos of these meals through MyFitnessPal, LoseIt!, CalAI, and Appediet. All four underestimated calorie content by 250 to 345 calories on average and undercounted fat by about 30 grams.

"People using a photo-based tracking app without adjusting the portions or entering the amounts of food should take the results with a grain of salt. These apps tend to underestimate calories, especially from fats, so what they actually ate is likely higher than what the app shows."

— Aaron Hengist, Postdoctoral Fellow, NIDDK/NIH

MyFitnessPal and LoseIt! performed better on higher-calorie meals than lower-calorie ones. All four apps estimated carbohydrates more consistently than other macronutrients. When researchers tested an additional 200 meals, they found accuracy dropped further for low-carb ketogenic diets, where higher fat content was consistently missed.

The Asian and Indian Food Problem

The NIH findings build on a University of Sydney study that screened 800 nutrition apps and evaluated 18 in detail across Western, Asian, and recommended diet plans. Led by Dr Juliana Chen, the research found that manual food-logging apps underestimated energy intake for Asian diets by an average of 1,520 kilojoules (about 363 calories).

AI-powered apps fared even worse on mixed Asian dishes. Calories for beef pho were overestimated by 49%, while pearl milk tea saw calorie underestimations of up to 76%.

"This issue is more common with Asian dishes, which usually contain a variety of mixed components that may not be found in the respective app's database, leading to possible errors when calculating the energy amount of a particular meal."

— Dr Juliana Chen, University of Sydney

The pattern extends directly to Indian cuisine. Dishes like biryani, dal makhani, and chole bhature — which combine grains, legumes, fats, and spices in layered preparations — are exactly the kind of mixed-component meals that confuse AI recognition systems. When an app can't distinguish ghee-laden rice from plain steamed rice, or identify the cream content in a paneer dish, the calorie gap can be enormous.

Why the AI Gets It Wrong

The core issue isn't that AI doesn't know nutrition facts. Independent testing by researcher Aleksey Treschilov, who ran 66 food photos through AI models, found that calorie-per-100-gram knowledge was accurate 96.7% of the time when checked against USDA reference tables.

The real weakness is portion weight estimation. AI models frequently confuse the state of food — treating cooked grains as if they were dry. One cup of dry rice contains about 700 calories; one cup of cooked rice, roughly 200. If the model silently assumes "dry," the calorie count triples. For rice-heavy Indian meals, this error alone could throw off a full day's tracking.

Fat is another blind spot. At nine calories per gram — more than double protein or carbs — even small errors in fat detection multiply quickly. Cooking oils, ghee, and butter are difficult for image recognition to detect, yet they dominate the calorie profile of many Indian preparations.

What This Means for Health-Conscious Eaters

For the millions using apps like HealthifyMe, MyFitnessPal, or newer AI-powered trackers to manage weight or monitor conditions like diabetes, the message is clear: treat photo-based estimates as rough guides, not precise measurements.

The NIH researchers recommend combining photo-based tracking with traditional methods — manually entering portion sizes and cross-referencing with known values. Dr Chen's team goes further, calling on app developers to engage dietitians in development, train AI models on diverse food images (particularly mixed and culturally varied dishes), and expand food composition databases beyond Western-centric entries.

India's app-based health tracking market has boomed in recent years, with platforms like HealthifyMe and cult.fit building large user bases around AI-driven food logging. These findings suggest that users — especially those tracking calories for medical reasons like managing diabetes or post-bariatric surgery nutrition — should verify estimates rather than trust them at face value.

What's Next

The NIH team plans further research into what specific meal characteristics affect app accuracy most. Meanwhile, the push for culturally diverse training data is gaining momentum. Until AI catches up, the old-fashioned kitchen scale remains the most reliable calorie counter — whether you're measuring out rajma chawal or a ketogenic dinner.
